pr_title: Daemon fix double kills of collection threads on shutdown
pr_body:
<!--
Describe the change in summary section, including rationale and degin decisions.
Include "Fixes #nnn" if you are fixing an existing issue.

In "Component Name" section write which component is changed in this PR. This
will help us review your PR quicker.

If you have more information you want to add, write them in "Additional
Information" section. This is usually used to help others understand your
motivation behind this change. A step-by-step reproduction of the problem is
helpful if there is no related issue.

##### Summary
Disables collection threads killed with `SIGTERM` to stop the cleanup function from attempting to kill them again.

##### Component Name
daemon

##### Additional Information
Fixes #6190
pr_comments:
[![CLA assistant check](https://cla-assistant.io/pull/badge/signed)](https://cla-assistant.io/netdata/netdata?pullRequest=6387)
All committers have signed the CLA.

Why did you reverse success and failure cases?

Why don't you use `else` instead of `if(code != 0)`?
What is the reason for the extensive usage of `goto exit_code_analyzed;`?

First of all, a disclaimer: this is what I, personally, think is better. If the project's style is agreed upon and should be maintained, then I'll discard this commit as non-essential (as it says in the commit message).

The reason is purely stylistic: this way the code reads more like English (as in, a natural language), and is therefore easier to understand. Instead of figuring out nested `if - else`'s that sometimes take their first branches on `true`s and sometimes on `false`s, I would argue that a more straightforward approach makes these various cases more comprehensible.

For me it reads, for example: "the error code is 0, and there are successful collections - everything is fine; if there aren't, and the collector hadn't failed too much, retry; if it had - disable it.". Now compare that with the previous version.

`goto`s are just a way to organize this without the nesting. 

I tried to rewrite this code for humans to read, but it still should be just as performant: the most often (if I understand the module's way of operation correctly) case of "everything is fine" is denoted as `likely` and positioned closer to the entry point; all the `goto`s and other `if`s (and the absence of an `else` that you are concerned about) are very straightforward for the compiler to optimize. I took a look at the assembly, it seems adequate.

So, to recap, I strongly believe this is just better to read, and there are no other side-effects. There also aren't any other reasons for this refactoring.

What's you opinion, @vlvkobal?

> There also aren't any other reasons for this refactoring.

i see no `refactoring` part in the OP

> Disables collection threads killed with SIGTERM to stop the cleanup function from attempting to kill them again.

Maybe it should be there with motives. I agree that nested if/else is (always) hard to read/follow. 

If there is a willing to make it readable (which is very nice), then it would be nice to have it w/o goto's. My 2 cents.
Trying to fix nested if/else is a good intention imo, thumbs up for it :+1:

Thank you all for the review!

I took most of your advice: success and error handling are now separate functions, no more `goto`s... but haven't returned the comments. Do we really want them anymore when the conditions are so simple?

Also, the build now fails because
```
The command "sudo apt-get install -y libcap2-bin zlib1g-dev uuid-dev fakeroot libipmimonitoring-dev libmnl-dev libnetfilter-acct-dev gnupg python-pip" failed and exited with 100 during .
```

> Do we really want them anymore when the conditions are so simple?

i would say no. I see no reason to have them after refactoring.
@cakrit @vlvkobal are you OK with this PR? Are there any other issues you'd like me to address here?

issue_context.title: charts.d kills process twice
issue_context.body:
<!---
When creating a bug report please:

- Write which component is affected. We group our components the same way our
  code is structured so basically:
  component name = dir in top level directory of repository
- Describe how you found this bug and how we can reproduce it. Preferable with
  a minimal test-case scenario. You can paste gist.github.com links for larger
  files
- Provide a clear and concise description of what you expected to happen.
-->

##### Bug report summary
The following show up in the error.log every time netdata is stopped:
`systemctl stop netdata`
or
`systemctl restart netdata`
or
`reboot`

> 2019-06-01 07:48:55: netdata ERROR : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : read failed
2019-06-01 07:48:55: netdata ERROR : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : '/usr/libexec/netdata/plugins.d/charts.d.plugin' (pid 27374) disconnected after 50 successful data collections (ENDs).
2019-06-01 07:48:56: netdata INFO  : PLUGINSD : stopping plugin thread: plugin:charts.d
2019-06-01 07:48:56: netdata INFO  : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : data collection thread exiting
2019-06-01 07:48:56: netdata INFO  : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : killing child process pid 27374
2019-06-01 07:48:56: netdata ERROR : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : Request to kill pid 27374, but it is not running. (errno 3, No such process)
2019-06-01 07:48:56: netdata INFO  : PLUGINSD[charts.d] : thread with task id 27366 finished

This doesn't really affect netdata running but it does fill up the logs with errors that make it harder to troubleshoot what is really going wrong with a plugin.

It seems like when a shutdown command is given:
/collectors/plugins.d/plugins_d.c keeps trying to read and produces the "read failed" error.
/collectors/plugins.d/plugins_d.c sends the "disconnected after xx successful data collections (ENDs)" error.
This is produced whenever any plugin (charts.d, python.d, etc) exits so I'm guessing it is intended.
collectors/plugins.d/plugins_d.c then attempts to stop the process by calling "killpid" from /daemon/main.c
Somewhere the process has already been killed so /daemon/main.c sends the error "(errno 3, No such process)"

##### OS / Environment
Ubuntu 18.04 headless server

##### Netdata version (ouput of `netdata -V`)
netdata v1.15.0-42-nightly

##### Component Name
/collectors/charts.d.plugin/charts.d.plugin.in

##### Steps To Reproduce
Disable all modules except apcupsd or sensors in charts.d.conf (sensors disabled in python.d.conf)
Note: I have tested this with only apcupsd or sensors modules enabled. Both individually produce the same errors on exit. So I'm assuming the errors do not have to do with the modules but with the charts.d plugin
`systemctl stop netdata.service`
`truncate -s 0 /var/log/netdata/error.log`
`systemctl start netdata.service`
No errors will show on start.
`systemctl stop netdata.service`
All the above errors show.


##### Expected behavior
Stop or restart without causing exit errors.
comments: Thanks @Steve8291 . Not the highest priority, but very good report and what you say makes sense. I'll see what we can do...

review_comments: It's due to it being a pthread function, see [pthread_create](http://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_create.3.html).

Hm, i think the whole plugin exit/restart handling logic is a little bit lame.
For example why do we need to `sleep((unsigned int) (cd->update_every * 10)` if `!cd->enabled` ?

should we even pass `cd` to handle func if it is disabled after `pluginsd_process`? :thinking: 	

i suggest to dig into it and see if there is any logic problems. Could you do it @emmrk?
^^ this should be another PR tho

Well yes, there's at least this one unnecessary `sleep`... I've made it into an issue (https://github.com/netdata/netdata/issues/6402) so that it's not lost (is that a good idea?). I'll probably look into it later
